an1.209:1.1: Rāhula was the Buddha’s son to his wife Bhaddakaccānā ([an1.245]()). Rāhula’s going forth is related at [pli-tv-kd1:54.1.1](), and other important discourses with him include [mn61](), [mn62](), and [mn147]() = [sn35.121](). In the latter he became an arahant, which he confirmed in his own words at [thag4.8](). Commentaries explain his name as meaning “bondage”, but it probably refers rather to being born under the influence of the dark star Rāhu ([sn2.8]()). His desire for training is illustrated in a series of lessons through which Rāhula doggedly persists ([sn18.1]()). His death is not noted in the early texts.
an1.210:1.1: The story of Raṭṭhapāla, the “guardian of the nation”, has become one of the most famous and beloved parables from early Buddhism ([mn82]()). It is a testament to a young man’s resolution to go forth out of faith.
an1.211:1.1: Kuṇḍadhāna has a single verse, which however has nothing to do with this subject ([thag1.15]()), and he may be listed along with Sakyan monks at [mn68:2.2.](). Apart from this it is not clear why he has this honor; the commentarial story is absurd. Saṅgha procedures normally require consensus from the community that is present. In certain situations, however, a vote may be performed. Votes were tallied by distributing “ballot slips” (_salāka_). The one who manages the process must be of exemplary character ([pli-tv-kd14:9.1.1]()).
an1.217:1.1: “Kassapa the Prince” (Kumārakassapa) was ordained at twenty ([pli-tv-kd1:75.1.1]()). He features in the Pāyāsisutta ([dn23]()), the Vammikasutta ([mn23]()), and his verses are collected in the Theragāthā ([thag2.41]()). His distinction here is apparently in recognition of the elaborate skills displayed in the Pāyāsisutta. Since that sutta begins without mentioning the Buddha, however, it was probably spoken after the Buddha’s passing (see commentary to Vimānavatthu 74), so his addition here must have been later still.
